seo.metaDescription: In a review of AI in eye care, 27 of 29 results top 90%. What is really stopping it in UK practice, and who carries the risk.
seo.metaTitle: AI in eye care: who is liable when it is wrong

keyPoints: A systematic review of AI reading fundus photographs lists 27 of 29 results above 90% in its table, and finds three barriers: workflow and cost, black-box outputs, models that do not generalise.
It does not answer the liability question. A UK commission said eight days earlier that negligence claims are disproportionately likely to be brought against clinicians and providers.
In the GOC's 2026 survey, 76% of optometrists were concerned about their legal responsibility if AI gets it wrong, as many as about AI errors, and 65% rated their AI knowledge poor.
The change a practice can make this week is a record: what the AI provided, how it informed the decision, and when and why you preferred your own reasoning.

faq.a: A fundus camera photographs the back of the eye: the retina, optic disc and macula. Those images are what diabetic eye screening grades, and they are what the AI systems in this review were reading. The review excluded studies using OCT or the slit lamp, though at least two systems in its own performance table use OCT as well as fundus images.
faq.q: What is a fundus camera?

faq.a: Software that reads retinal photographs and flags the ones that look abnormal, either as a first grader or as a triage step before a person looks. In research it performs well: 27 of the 29 results in this review's performance table are above 90%. In UK practice it is still rare: in the General Optical Council's 2026 survey, 8% of working registrants said they used AI of any kind to support a diagnosis, and 60% used it for none of the tasks listed.
faq.q: What is AI fundus screening?

faq.a: Not in the English programme. A 2020 independent evaluation of the EyeArt algorithm read 30,405 consecutive episodes across three English programmes and found referable retinopathy with 95.7% sensitivity, classifying all 462 cases of moderate-to-severe or proliferative disease as test-positive, including images it could not read. It agreed with the human grade of non-referable in only 54.0%, and its authors were testing it alongside human grading, not in place of it. Scotland's programme then used a computer to triage macular images. The UK National Screening Committee still did not recommend automated grading on 1 October 2026; its consultation closed on 3 August.
faq.q: Does the NHS use AI for diabetic eye screening?

faq.a: That depends on the facts, and it is not settled. What the National Commission into the Regulation of AI in Healthcare found in September 2026 is that negligence claims are disproportionately likely to be brought against healthcare professionals and providers, because they hold the clearest duty of care, which it calls a perceived liability sink. Its Recommendation 28 asks that the contract between manufacturer and provider set out who delivers which risk controls. The College of Optometrists is plain about the clinical side: responsibility for the decision stays with the clinician, who must keep oversight and be able to overrule the software.
faq.q: Who is liable if an AI tool gets a diagnosis wrong?

body.text: AI in eye care does well in research. [A systematic review published on 18 September in the International Journal of Ophthalmology](https://doi.org/10.18240/ijo.2026.09.17) read 34 studies of AI reading fundus photographs. In its own performance table, 27 of the 29 results are above 90%, though the column it labels accuracy also holds sensitivities and an area under the curve.

What it does not answer is who carries the risk. It names medicolegal liability as a concern, but its results give three barriers and no analysis of who is liable. Eight days earlier, an independent commission set up by the MHRA reported on exactly that, and the GOC says it will respond.
What the review did

A PRISMA review, not a meta-analysis. Scopus, PubMed and Web of Science were searched to June 2025, and 34 studies were included, three of them from the UK. Diabetic retinopathy was the commonest subject, in 25 of them. Studies using OCT or the slit lamp were excluded. On the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool, 22 studies were moderate to high quality and 12 showed notable limitations.
What it found, and what it left out

Three barriers. The software does not fit the working day: separate programs, manual uploads, hardware that costs money. Clinicians cannot see how a black box reached its answer, which the authors tie to low trust. And models trained on one population do not travel, so performance falls in the groups already least well served. Their summary is blunt.
AI performs well in research (>90% accuracy) but falters in real-world use.

One hospital's simulation put numbers on the trade. [A study published in PLOS Digital Health on 15 September](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pdig.0001700) let AI clear its own negatives on 6,904 fundus photographs read by three retina specialists. The images needing a specialist fell to 7.3%–8.0% for diabetic retinopathy, and mean sensitivity for it fell from 0.9168 to 0.8838. In an exploratory analysis across all three diseases, 27.7%–30.1% still needed one. A stricter threshold won back most of the diabetic retinopathy loss, so where to set it is a clinical judgement as much as a technical one.
Who is liable when AI in eye care is wrong

[The National Commission into the Regulation of AI in Healthcare](https://www.gov.uk/government/publications/national-commission-into-the-regulation-of-ai-in-healthcare-recommendations-for-a-future-regulatory-framework/national-commission-into-the-regulation-of-ai-in-healthcare-recommendations-for-a-future-regulatory-framework) reported on 10 September with 44 recommendations. Under negligence as it stands, it found, claims are disproportionately likely to be brought against healthcare professionals and providers, because they have the clearest duty of care. It calls the result a perceived “liability sink”. Recommendation 28 is that the contract between manufacturer and provider should set out who delivers which risk controls. That is a recommendation, not a requirement.

Optometrists have worked this out. In [the General Optical Council's 2026 registrant survey](https://optical.org/asset/7A4BF5B9%2D81F5%2D4657%2DBEC485376F5C1ED3/), 76% of the 2,064 optometrists who answered were concerned about their legal responsibility if something goes wrong, as many as were concerned about the AI making errors, and 65% rated their own knowledge of AI as poor.
Why it matters in practice

What changes is not the consulting room but what you ask a supplier and what you write down. [The College of Optometrists' interim position](https://www.college-optometrists.org/policy-and-influencing/position-statements/interim-position-on-the-use-of-ai) says, among other things, three you can act on. Check the tool is registered with the MHRA as Artificial Intelligence as a Medical Device before you buy it. Tell patients when AI is being used, and where possible let them opt out. And keep records of what the AI provided, how it informed the decision, and when and why you preferred your own reasoning. That last one you can do this week.

The contract is the next renewal's job. The third is what to tell the patient who asks whether a computer will read their photographs. In NHS diabetic eye screening in England it will not yet, though the UK National Screening Committee is closer than it was: the evidence summary it consulted on concludes that some systems are as good as a first human grader and could be tested in real NHS services. That consultation closed on 3 August 2026, and no updated recommendation had been published by 1 October. For anything else, the answer is whatever your own practice's software does. What reaches the high street, to my mind, arrives inside a pathway, as [Denmark's OCT roll-out](/news/denmark-oct-teleophthalmology-referrals) did, not as a box on its own.
The caveats

items: The review's arithmetic does not hold together: the abstract says 34 studies from 2018 to 2025, the results say 2016 to 2025, and the table lists 29 entries, nine of them dated 2026. One of those reads fundus and OCT together, which its own exclusion criteria rule out. It states no limitations of its own.

The table's figures are each entry's own, mostly on curated data, never pooled, and not all are accuracies: some are sensitivities, one an area under the curve. Two rows cite reviews; the lowest, 73.0%, cites a news report. One model fell from 98.84% to 87.13% on outside data. None measures sight saved.
The Commission is an independent expert advisory body set up by the MHRA. Its 44 recommendations are not law, the government response is still to come, and the liability passage is analysis, not law.

The GOC figures are self-reported by the 3,451 who answered, an 11% response rate. The triage simulation is single-centre, retrospective and Korean, part-funded by the software's maker, two of whose employees are authors.

seo.metaDescription: What goes into an optometrist referral, from 104,190 e-referrals in Greater Manchester: glaucoma first, 10.2% with no subspecialty, and what goes missing.
seo.metaTitle: Optometrist referral: what the hospital needs to see

keyPoints: In 104,190 electronic referrals from Greater Manchester optometrists, June 2022 to May 2024, glaucoma was the commonest reason, at 12.2%, ahead of other medical retina, YAG capsulotomy and cataract.
10.2% went to hospital as "Not Otherwise Specified", with no subspecialty, and 3.0% went to glaucoma enhanced services, a figure the authors say understates scheme use.
In a Canadian audit of 522 glaucoma referrals, optometrists' were the more complete, but visual fields and OCT were among the elements most often missing.
In Bradford, 39.8% of suspected wet AMD referrals were confirmed, yet 76.8% of those made before the pandemic were judged necessary.

faq.a: The College of Optometrists' guidance (C206) says a referral should include the relevant details from the eye examination, the reason for referral with images where appropriate, details of discussions with the patient and any with the practitioner being referred to, and the level of urgency. In a Canadian review of 522 glaucoma referrals, visual fields and OCT were among the elements most often left out.
faq.q: What should an optometrist referral letter include?

faq.a: In 104,190 electronic referrals from optometrists in Greater Manchester between June 2022 and May 2024, glaucoma was the commonest reason, at 12.2%, followed by other medical retina at 11.6%, YAG laser capsulotomy at 11.1% and cataract at 10.8%. The authors note cataract is likely to be undercounted, because referrals through the enhanced cataract scheme use a separate form.
faq.q: What are the most common reasons optometrists refer to an ophthalmologist?

faq.a: In a study of 394 referrals to one specialist macular treatment centre, in Bradford between 2019 and 2021, 39.8% of referrals for suspected wet AMD were confirmed, and the commonest misdiagnosis was dry AMD. Other UK studies the authors cite found 37% in the Highlands and 26% in Wales. Most referrals were still warranted: 76.8% of the suspected wet AMD referrals made before the pandemic led to treatment or observation over several visits.
faq.q: How accurate are optometrist referrals for wet AMD?

faq.a: Often not. The Bradford authors cite a study in which the reply rate to optometrists' referrals was 2.6%, and the Manchester team suggest that delayed or absent replies from hospital may prompt glaucoma re-referrals. Without a reply, the optometrist cannot learn whether the proposed diagnosis was right.
faq.q: Do optometrists get a reply to their referrals?

body.text: What its authors call the first large-scale analysis of electronic optometry referrals in the UK was [published in Ophthalmic and Physiological Optics on 26 September](https://doi.org/10.1007/s44402-026-00198-x). Researchers in Manchester looked at 104,190 referrals from Greater Manchester optometrists between June 2022 and May 2024. Glaucoma was the commonest reason for an optometrist referral, and 10.2% of all the referrals were sent to hospital as "Not Otherwise Specified", with no subspecialty named.
Most earlier studies, the authors note, looked at one condition at a time. Two such studies show what the hospital finds in glaucoma and wet AMD referrals, and the numbers cut both ways.
What the study did

It is a retrospective service evaluation of routinely collected data from the NHS England North West Electronic Eyecare Referral System, limited to referrals from Greater Manchester. The authors described where referrals went and why, and tested how deprivation, age, sex and ethnicity related to each type, with deprivation and ethnicity measured by area rather than per patient.
What 104,190 optometrist referrals showed

81.8% went to hospital ophthalmology: 71.6% to a named clinic type and 10.2% as "Not Otherwise Specified", an option on the form for when the referrer cannot settle on a diagnosis or no clinic type fits. 15.0% went to GPs, and 3.0% to glaucoma enhanced services in the community.

Glaucoma led, at 12.2% (12,777 referrals), then other medical retina at 11.6%, YAG laser capsulotomy at 11.1% and cataract at 10.8%. Cataract and paediatric binocular vision referrals came more often from more deprived areas, and vitreoretinal, adult binocular vision and other medical retina from less deprived ones.

The authors say the figures suggest, rather than confirm, that community schemes were underused. They also set out why glaucoma is hard to refer well: a GOS sight test is time-limited and does not routinely include visual fields, OCT or gonioscopy, so a referral made outside an enhanced scheme often rests on a single clinical impression, and referring when uncertain may be the safest choice for the patient.
What the hospital finds missing

[A Dalhousie University team](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/42419692/) scored 522 referrals to two glaucoma specialists in 2024. Optometrists' referrals were the more complete, with a median score of 9 against 5 for ophthalmologists', but visual fields and OCT were among the elements most often missing from both, and optometrists more often left out ocular history and medications. 33.9% of patients referred by optometrists had an intervention at the first visit, against 59.7% of those referred by ophthalmologists. The abstract does not define an intervention, and the comparison is unadjusted, so the gap may reflect who is referred as much as how.

[In Bradford](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC11976509/), a review of 394 referrals to a specialist macular treatment centre found the letters themselves were good: legibility was high, and distance acuity was recorded in 99.0% before the pandemic. But 39.8% of referrals for suspected wet AMD were confirmed, the commonest misdiagnosis being dry AMD. Even so, 76.8% of the suspected wet AMD referrals made before the pandemic were judged necessary, because the patient was treated or observed over several visits.
For a system that puts OCT and a consultant's reading behind the referral, see [Denmark's optician stores](/news/denmark-oct-teleophthalmology-referrals).
Why it matters in practice

items: Name the clinic when you can, and keep "Not Otherwise Specified" for when no diagnosis or clinic type fits.

Send what the College asks for: the relevant findings, the reason for referral with images where appropriate, what you discussed with the patient, and the urgency ([Guidance for Professional Practice, C206](https://www.college-optometrists.org/clinical-guidance/guidance/communication,-partnership-and-teamwork/working-with-colleagues/referrals)). For signs of possible glaucoma at a routine sight test, the College notes that NICE recommends additional tests before referral (C195).
For suspected wet AMD, the acuity carries weight: in Bradford, reduced visual acuity was the sign most strongly linked to a confirmed diagnosis, followed by haemorrhage.
Use the glaucoma scheme where one is commissioned. Only 3.0% of the Manchester referrals went to one, a figure the authors say understates use.

Ask for the reply. The Bradford authors cite a study in which the reply rate to optometrists' referrals was 2.6%, and the Manchester team suggest delayed or absent replies may prompt glaucoma re-referrals. Without a reply, the optometrist never learns whether the diagnosis was right.

The government's £20 million plan aims to give every optical practice with an NHS contract in England [access to the NHS e-Referral Service](https://www.gov.uk/government/news/millions-to-get-faster-eye-care-on-the-high-street) by April 2028.

body.text: The caveats

items: The Manchester data count referral events, not patients or outcomes, and nothing in them says whether a referral was right.

Repeat referrals could not be linked, and the authors say re-referral may inflate glaucoma's count. Referrals made inside enhanced schemes use a separate form and were not captured, so glaucoma, cataract and scheme use are likely to be undercounted. Glaucoma's lead over other medical retina is narrow, and the authors read the ranking as a pattern of recorded referral activity.
The Canadian figures come from the abstract, as the full paper could not be opened, and its clinics and funding differ from the UK's.
The Bradford study is one centre, from March 2019 to February 2021, half of it during the pandemic.

seo.metaDescription: A global model puts sight loss from AMD at 21.34 million by 2050. What the stage split means for macular degeneration in the UK, where 1 in 8 at 80 has it.
seo.metaTitle: Macular degeneration in the UK: the 2050 forecast

keyPoints: The Global Burden of Disease 2021 analysis projects vision impairment from AMD to rise from 8.06 million people in 2021 to 21.34 million by 2050. Both ends are modelled estimates, not counts.
A model published on 18 September puts global prevalence of intermediate AMD at 4.01%, against 0.32% for geographic atrophy and 0.31% for neovascular AMD, with no age range stated.
Rates per head are falling. Global age-standardised prevalence of that sight loss fell 5.53% between 1990 and 2021, western Europe's by about 20%. Totals rise with ageing and population growth.
The UK sits inside those global models as one of 204 countries. The UK-specific study underneath our own figures is from 2012 and stops at 2020, at 679,000 late AMD cases.

faq.a: There is no recent count. The UK-specific estimate this article uses is a 2012 modelling study in the British Journal of Ophthalmology, which applied prevalence from 31 population studies to Office for National Statistics figures and found late AMD in 2.4% of people aged 50 and over, about 513,000 cases, rising to 679,000 by 2020. The authors stopped there on purpose, saying population data beyond 2020 may be less reliable. Prevalence climbs steeply with age: 4.8% at 65 and over, and 12.2% at 80 and over, roughly 1 in 8. Global models published since do cover the UK, but they fit it as one of 204 countries rather than from UK data.
faq.q: How many people have macular degeneration in the UK?

faq.a: Intermediate AMD is the stage between early changes and late disease, marked by large drusen or pigmentary change, usually with acuity still reasonable. A model published in Ophthalmology Retina on 18 September 2026 puts its global prevalence at 4.01%, against 0.32% for geographic atrophy and 0.31% for neovascular AMD. That is about six times as many people at the intermediate stage as at both late stages combined, and it is the stage with nothing licensed to offer. The abstract states no age range for those percentages, so they are whole-population figures rather than the rate in a clinic of older patients.
faq.q: What is intermediate AMD and how common is it?

faq.a: Nothing is licensed for early or intermediate AMD. For geographic atrophy, the first candidate did not get through: the European Medicines Agency confirmed its refusal of pegcetacoplan (Syfovre) on 19 September 2024, and the MHRA rejected it for the UK, which the Macular Society called a disappointing decision for people living with the condition. Writing in January 2025, the society said a second complement drug, avacincaptad pegol, was under consideration by the MHRA, so check the current position before you tell a patient anything. Anti-VEGF injections treat neovascular AMD only. For everyone else the offer is monitoring, advice on smoking and diet, and support.
faq.q: Is there any treatment for dry macular degeneration in the UK?

body.text: The world has a new forecast for age-related macular degeneration: 21.34 million people with sight loss by 2050, against 8.06 million in 2021. Both come from the [Global Burden of Disease 2021 analysis of AMD](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12208786/) in The Lancet Global Health, and both are modelled estimates rather than counts. What it means for macular degeneration in the UK turns on a second paper, published this month.

That study, [published in Ophthalmology Retina on 18 September](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.oret.2026.09.019), re-sorted the world's prevalence studies into one classification, Beckman, and reported the stages separately. Jeong and colleagues, mostly in Seoul, with L Smith at Anglia Ruskin in Cambridge. It is paywalled, so everything here comes from its abstract.
What the two studies did

Both are burden models, not trials, and neither examined a new patient. The GBD analysis used 163 rapid assessment surveys and 107 other population studies to model 204 countries from 1990 to 2021. It counted only moderate to severe vision loss and blindness, acuity worse than 6/18, and forecast to 2050 with an ensemble of 12 submodels. The Gates Foundation funded it, among others, with no role in the work.

The Ophthalmology Retina paper is a systematic review modelled with DisMod-MR. The original studies did not use Beckman, so an expectation-maximisation algorithm split the pooled prevalence into early, intermediate, geographic atrophy and neovascular disease. The two measure different things: sight loss caused by AMD, and the disease at any stage.
What was found

Vision impairment from AMD more than doubled between 1990 and 2021, from 3.64 million people to 8.06 million, and is projected to reach 21.34 million by 2050: 9.02 million males (95% uncertainty interval 5.72 to 14.20) and 12.32 million females (8.88 to 17.08). Rates per head went the other way. Global age-standardised prevalence of that impairment fell 5.53% over the period, western Europe's from 107.40 to 85.55 per 100,000, about 20%. The totals rise with ageing and population growth, not with severity.

The stage split matters more in clinic. In 2021 the Beckman model put global prevalence of AMD at any stage at 10.03%: early 5.40%, intermediate 4.01%, geographic atrophy 0.32% and neovascular AMD 0.31%. For every person at a late stage there are about six at the intermediate stage, with large drusen, acuity still reasonable and nothing licensed to offer them. The abstract states no age range, so those are whole-population figures, not the rate in a chair.
Why it matters for macular degeneration in the UK

The UK sits inside both models as one of 204 countries, fitted from a worldwide evidence base rather than from UK data. Our own study is older. Owen and colleagues, in the [British Journal of Ophthalmology in 2012](https://doi.org/10.1136/bjophthalmol-2011-301109), applied prevalence from 31 population studies to ONS figures and estimated 513,000 people with late AMD, 2.4% of those aged 50 and over, rising to 4.8% at 65 and 12.2% at 80, roughly 1 in 8. They put 71,200 new cases a year on it and projected 679,000 by 2020, stopping there because data beyond that point may be less reliable.
The Royal College of Ophthalmologists' commissioning guidance has already decided who monitors them:
Do not routinely monitor people with early AMD or late AMD (dry) at HES unless in clinical research.

That guidance uses the NICE classification, which has no intermediate category, so the Beckman stages do not map onto it cleanly. It says those patients continue to attend routine sight tests with their primary care optometrist, and that OCT is the most sensitive monitoring tool, naming it for community provision in patients at high risk of new neovascular AMD or monitored for stable neovascular AMD. [Denmark's community OCT programme](/news/denmark-oct-teleophthalmology-referrals) is the other half of that arithmetic.

Three things follow. When wet AMD is suspected, speed is the whole job: NICE's quality standard expects treatment within 14 days of referral to the macular service, and the Royal College asks for acuity, fundoscopy findings and the OCT images in the letter. Second, the smoking conversation is for everyone: tobacco accounted for 18.72% of male disability-adjusted life years from AMD against 3.89% of female, a gap the paper puts down to how many men smoked, not to a different macula. Third, the European Medicines Agency confirmed its refusal of pegcetacoplan on 19 September 2024 and the MHRA rejected it here too, so the first candidate treatment for geographic atrophy never reached UK patients.
The caveats

items: Both papers are models. The 21.34 million adds two point estimates whose 95% uncertainty intervals run 5.72 to 14.20 million males and 8.88 to 17.08 million females.
They count different things: GBD counts sight loss from AMD, at acuity worse than 6/18, Beckman the disease at any stage.
The Ophthalmology Retina paper is paywalled, so only its abstract could be read here, it gives no 2050 figure, and its stages are imputed, not observed.
GBD modelled smoking alone as a risk factor, could not separate wet from dry disease without fundus photography, and says the burden may be underestimated.
The UK estimate is from 2012, from studies in white populations, and assumes AMD is lifelong and mortality unchanged by it.

seo.metaDescription: Sight loss statistics for England: glaucoma certifications rose from 1,648 to 2,645 a year since 2009/10 while diabetic eye disease fell. What that means.
seo.metaTitle: Sight loss statistics: glaucoma certificates in England

keyPoints: In England, certificates of vision impairment for glaucoma rose from 1,648 (7.3% of all) in 2009/10 to 2,645 (10.7%) in 2024/25, a study in Eye reported on 16 September.
Diabetic eye disease fell from 1,261 (5.6%) to 872 (3.5%), which the authors say screening and better treatment might explain. Glaucoma has no screening programme.
Worldwide in 2020, 77.3% of blindness and moderate or severe vision impairment was due to cataract or uncorrected refractive error, and 90.9% once uncorrected near vision is counted.
These are counts, not rates: an earlier analysis found no significant change in the glaucoma certification rate between 2010/11 and 2017/18.

faq.a: Worldwide, more than 90% of people with vision impairment have a preventable or treatable cause, according to the Lancet Global Health Commission on Global Eye Health. In 2020, 77.3% of blindness and moderate or severe vision impairment was due to cataract or uncorrected refractive error, rising to 90.9% when near vision impairment is included. England measures preventable sight loss through certificates of vision impairment for AMD, glaucoma and diabetic eye disease.
faq.q: What percentage of sight loss is avoidable?

faq.a: A CVI can be issued in England to someone who meets the criteria for sight impairment or severe sight impairment. It records the main cause of their sight loss and can help them reach support. With the patient's consent, a copy goes to the Royal College of Ophthalmologists' Certification Office at Moorfields Eye Hospital, which is how the national figures are counted.
faq.q: What is a Certificate of Vision Impairment (CVI)?

faq.a: Of the four causes a 2026 study tracked, AMD was the main cause on 9,833 certificates of vision impairment in England in 2024/25 (39.6%), glaucoma on 2,645 (10.7%), hereditary eye disease on 1,652 (6.7%) and diabetic eye disease on 872 (3.5%). About four in ten certificates name another main cause. Since 2009/10, AMD and diabetic eye disease have fallen as a share, and glaucoma and hereditary eye disease have risen.
faq.q: What are the main causes of certified sight loss in England?

faq.a: World Sight Day 2026 is on Thursday 8 October. The International Agency for the Prevention of Blindness runs it under the theme #LoveYourEyes, in the run-up to the Global Summit for Eye Health in Antigua and Barbuda on 2 November 2026.
faq.q: When is World Sight Day 2026?

body.text: More than 90% of people in the world with vision impairment have a cause that could have been prevented or treated, the [Lancet Global Health Commission on Global Eye Health](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC7966694/) found, and treatments for cataract and refractive error would meet more than 90% of the unmet need. England keeps its own sight loss statistics, and [a study published in Eye on 16 September](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41433-026-04882-7) has counted 16 years of them. Certificates of vision impairment for glaucoma rose from 1,648 in 2009/10 to 2,645 in 2024/25. Those for diabetic eye disease fell from 1,261 to 872.

Diabetic eye disease has a national screening programme in England. Glaucoma has none: [the UK National Screening Committee does not currently recommend screening for it](https://view-health-screening-recommendations.service.gov.uk/glaucoma/). And glaucoma is mostly asymptomatic until late, which is why, in most prevalence surveys from high-income countries, less than half of the glaucoma found had been diagnosed before. In the week of World Sight Day, on 8 October, that is a gap a UK sight test is placed to close.
What the study counted

A Certificate of Vision Impairment (CVI) can be given to someone in England who meets the criteria for sight impairment or severe sight impairment. It records the main cause and can help them reach support. With consent, a copy of every one goes to the Royal College of Ophthalmologists' Certification Office at Moorfields Eye Hospital.

A Moorfields and UCL team counted the certificates received each year from April 2009 to March 2025, in total and for four main causes: age-related macular degeneration (AMD), glaucoma, diabetic eye disease and hereditary eye disease. It is a one-page descriptive report. The same certificates are England's measure of preventable sight loss: [the Public Health Outcomes Framework reports them for AMD, glaucoma and diabetic eye disease](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41433-020-0864-6).
What the sight loss statistics show
Certificates rose from 22,687 in 2009/10 to 24,819 in 2023/24, with a dip to 16,499 in 2020/21, the year of the COVID-19 lockdowns. The paper gives no total for 2024/25.

AMD is still the largest cause, but its share fell, from 10,393 certificates (45.8%) in 2009/10 to 9,833 (39.6%) in 2024/25. This week's other article, on how AMD is forecast to grow to 2050, is on [our news page](/news).

Glaucoma went the other way, from 1,648 certificates (7.3%) to 2,645 (10.7%), and the paper's figure shows most of that rise after the 2020/21 dip. Diabetic eye disease fell from 1,261 (5.6%) to 872 (3.5%), the biggest proportionate fall of the four. Hereditary eye disease rose from 1,077 (4.7%) to 1,652 (6.7%), and has outnumbered diabetic eye disease every year since 2010/11.

The authors do not give a reason for the rise in glaucoma. Of diabetic eye disease they write that the fall "might reflect effective screening pathways and more efficacious treatments for diabetes and diabetic retinopathy".
Avoidable sight loss, worldwide and here

The Commission's figures for 2020 are 596 million people with distance vision impairment worldwide, of whom 43 million were blind, with cataract the leading cause of blindness at 17.01 million. Refractive error is not solved in high-income countries either: [effective refractive error coverage](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40414243/), the share of adults aged 50 and over who need distance correction and see well with it, was 84.0% in high-income countries in 2023, against 63.0% worldwide, both age-standardised modelled estimates.
Why it matters in practice

items: Look at the disc and record what you saw, including for the patient who came in for new glasses. Glaucoma has no national screening programme, and it is mostly asymptomatic until late.

By the time glaucoma reaches a certificate, the sight it has taken does not come back. The certificates cannot show how many of the 2,645 were found late, and the count rose over 16 years, most of it after 2020/21.

When a patient's sight has fallen to certification level and nobody has mentioned a CVI, ask the hospital. In one tertiary hospital cohort with diabetic retinopathy, 84% of those with vision impairment, by acuity, had no certificate after a mean follow-up of under two years.
Keep refraction in view. Effective coverage of 84.0% in high-income countries means about one in six adults over 50 who need distance correction still lack correction that gives them good vision.

body.text: The caveats

items: The counts depend on a certificate being offered and on consent, and the authors say they do not represent the full burden of visual impairment. Under-certification, as in the [UK hospital study of diabetic retinopathy](https://doi.org/10.1136/bjo-2022-321910), could mean national figures understate sight loss.

They are counts, not rates. The 2020 analysis of the same certificates found no statistically significant change in the glaucoma certification rate per 100,000 people aged 40 and over between 2010/11 and 2017/18, years in which the counts rose. The new report cannot say whether the risk has changed.
The explanation for diabetic eye disease is offered by the authors as a possibility, not shown, and AMD, which is not screened for, fell too.
The figures cover England only. The global figures are modelled estimates, for 2020 and 2023, not counts.

seo.metaDescription: A 95-trial network meta-analysis of atropine for myopia control ranks 0.01% 16th of 24, and measures the rebound 12 months after each treatment stops.
seo.metaTitle: Atropine for myopia control: what stopping costs

keyPoints: A Bayesian network meta-analysis of 95 randomised trials, funded by Santen, ranks childhood myopia treatments on what happens 12 months after stopping, which the authors say earlier analyses did not.
Stopping high-dose atropine cost −0.71 D against untreated controls. Stopping low-dose atropine cost −0.10 D, with the interval crossing zero. Red light, top at one year, rebounded 0.14 mm.
In the same paper's dose-response model, 0.01% atropine, the dose the MHRA licensed as Ryjunea, ranked 16th of 24 on refraction at one year, behind 0.025% at 10th.
NICE's appraisal of low-dose atropine stalled on 11 August 2026 when Santen asked for more time. The expected publication date is TBC, so the drop stays private for now.

faq.a: In the UK the licensed product, Ryjunea, is atropine 0.1 mg/ml, which is 0.01%, licensed for children of 3 to 14 with myopia between −0.50 DS and −6.00 DS progressing at 0.50 DS a year or more. The September network meta-analysis supports concentrations from 0.01% to 0.05% as the band with sustained two-year benefit and minimal rebound, and in its dose-response model 0.025% ranked 10th of 24 against 16th for 0.01% on refraction at one year. No other strength carries that licence, so a stronger concentration is prescribed outside it.
faq.q: What concentration of atropine is used for myopia control?

faq.a: It depends on the dose. Twelve months after stopping high-dose atropine, refraction had worsened by −0.71 D against untreated controls, and axial length by 0.20 mm. After low-dose atropine the difference was −0.10 D and 0.06 mm, with both credible intervals crossing zero, which the authors read as no rebound. In the paper's dose-response model the gradient ran through the concentrations: −0.20 D a year for 0.05%, −0.09 D for 0.025% and none for 0.01%.
faq.q: What happens when you stop atropine for myopia control?

faq.a: Not yet. Ryjunea is a prescription-only medicine available privately, and the College of Optometrists says it may be prescribed by independent prescribers with the relevant scope of practice, including IP optometrists and ophthalmologists competent in paediatric myopia management. NICE is appraising it for England, Wales and Northern Ireland, but that appraisal stalled on 11 August 2026 when Santen asked for more time to answer the draft guidance, and the expected publication date is now TBC. Scotland goes through the Scottish Medicines Consortium separately.
faq.q: Is low-dose atropine available on the NHS?

faq.a: The evidence does not settle it. A one-year trial of 504 children in Chengdu found ortho-k and the 7 mm CARE design both slowed axial growth more than the wider 9 mm design in moderate myopes, 0.16 mm and 0.19 mm against 0.25 mm, while nothing separated the three in low myopes. That trial was not randomised, was run at one centre, and only its abstract could be read. The network meta-analysis puts orthokeratology and multifocal lenses in a similar band to low-dose atropine, and warns that corneal reshaping confounds refraction, so axial length is the more informative measure for anything that reshapes the cornea.
faq.q: Is orthokeratology better than myopia control spectacle lenses?

body.text: Rank 23 childhood myopia treatments and an untreated control on a year's refraction change, and the dose licensed in the UK comes 16th. [The analysis](https://doi.org/10.1007/s40123-026-01478-y), published in Ophthalmology and Therapy on 7 September, pooled 95 randomised trials of atropine for myopia control and its optical and light-based rivals. Earlier syntheses ranked on treatment alone, the authors say. This one ranks on what happens 12 months after it stops too, and the order turns over.

That matters here. Ryjunea, atropine 0.1 mg/ml, is the first low-dose atropine the MHRA has licensed: children of 3 to 14, myopia between −0.50 DS and −6.00 DS, progressing at 0.50 DS a year or more. That is 0.01%, the bottom of the band this paper supports, and it is private-only: the NICE appraisal stalled on 11 August 2026 when Santen asked for more time on the draft guidance.
What the study did

Jovanović and colleagues found 117 randomised trials of 24 interventions in children under 18 with refraction worse than −0.50 D. Ninety-five went into the synthesis: 69 in the one-year refraction network, 80 in the axial-length network, eight in the post-cessation ones. Seventy-eight of the 117, 68 per cent, were run in East and Southeast Asia; eight were at low risk of bias throughout.
It was funded by Santen, whose drop is the licensed one: two of the seven authors are Santen employees, five IQVIA staff under contract.
What was found on atropine for myopia control

Rebound was extra progression in the 12 months after stopping, against untreated controls; over 0.25 D or 0.10 mm counted as meaningful. Stopping high-dose atropine (0.5% and above) cost −0.71 D (−1.13 to −0.31) and 0.20 mm of axial length, moderate-dose 0.19 mm. Low-dose atropine cost −0.10 D (−0.35 to 0.14) and 0.06 mm, multifocal soft lenses 0.01 mm, the intervals crossing zero.
After LDA discontinuation, progression was statistically and clinically indistinguishable from control for both SER and AL, indicating no rebound on either SER or AL.

In the dose-response model, which assumes higher doses do at least as much as lower ones, the gradient holds: −0.20 D a year for 0.05%, −0.09 D for 0.025%, none for 0.01%. And not only atropine: repeated low-intensity red light, the most effective on axial length at one year, rebounded 0.14 mm (0.02 to 0.26) once stopped, on one trial at high risk of bias and with no evidence of effect beyond year 1.

Effect during treatment runs the other way. In that same model, atropine split by concentration, 0.025% ranked 10th of the 24 and 0.01% 16th on refraction at one year, 0.025% beating it by 0.1 D (0.02 to 0.22). The licensed dose is the gentlest of the band, not the strongest, and the licence covers that strength alone: anything above sits outside it.
What the spectacle lens trials add

[A two-year randomised trial in Ophthalmology Science](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.xops.2026.101309), Zeiss-funded, followed 234 children aged 6 to 13 in Spain and Portugal, 208 to 24 months. Axial elongation was 0.21 mm in the CARE lens against 0.43 mm in single vision, and the split matters: 0.14 mm of benefit in year one, 0.08 mm in year two.

A second, non-randomised trial of 504 children in Chengdu compared orthokeratology with two designs of one lens. In moderate myopes, ortho-k and the 7 mm design gave 0.16 mm and 0.19 mm of axial growth against 0.25 mm for the 9 mm design; in low myopes nothing separated them. Only the abstract could be read, so nothing beyond it is claimed.
Why it matters in practice

Choose the exit at the same appointment as the entry. If a family starts something that rebounds, the stopping plan belongs in the consent conversation and the notes, not at 16. On 0.01% the honest framing is the smallest effect of the low doses and the cleanest stop.

Then measure axial length. The authors warn that corneal reshaping confounds refraction, and that axial length is the more informative measure for a cornea-modifying treatment. Which says to me that a practice fitting ortho-k without a biometer cannot audit its outcomes: the same case for equipment that [Denmark's high-street OCT data](/news/denmark-oct-teleophthalmology-referrals) made for imaging.

And say what is not known. Combining 0.01% atropine with orthokeratology was among the three most effective at one year and beat low-dose atropine alone over two years, with no post-cessation data. The College of Optometrists says combined therapy "is based on a limited number of trials with a low level of certainty".
The caveats

items: Funded by Santen, whose 0.01% drop is the licensed UK product. It calls its results indirect comparisons resting on modelling assumptions, not prescribing guidance.
The rebound networks rest on eight trials, more than one only for low-dose and high-dose atropine; the red light and contact lens figures on one each.
Confidence in the one-year refraction estimates was mostly low or very low. Chinese regional databases were not searched, safety not pooled, cost out of scope.
The lens trial lost 14 children from the single-vision arm against 4 from the lens arm in year two. The ortho-k comparison was non-randomised, single-centre and abstract-only.

keyPoints: In Scotland's orthoptist-led screening of children aged 3.5 to 5.5, squint rose from 1.42% in 2013–14 to 2.19% in 2021–22, mostly intermittent exotropia.
Binocular vision anomalies as the study defined them rose from 3.02% to 4.89%, with esophoria doubling. 512 children in 2021–22 would have passed a vision-only screen.
NICE: a new squint with a lost red reflex, or with ataxia, vomiting or headache, is referred immediately. The College treats a new or sudden squint as a 24-hour emergency.
Some orthoptists refract children in hospital clinics, but only optometrists and registered medical practitioners can issue a UK spectacle prescription.

faq.a: Orthoptists specialise in eye movements and binocular vision, work mainly in hospital eye departments and deliver children's vision screening where eye care professionals do it, as in Scotland. Optometrists work mainly in community practice and carry out sight tests. Some orthoptists refract, mostly young children in hospital clinics, but under the Opticians Act only optometrists and registered medical practitioners can issue a spectacle prescription, so an ophthalmologist or optometrist signs it.
faq.q: What is the difference between an orthoptist and an optometrist?

faq.a: NICE's guideline sets the route. A new squint with loss of the red reflex goes to ophthalmology immediately, and a new squint with ataxia, vomiting or headache to acute paediatric services immediately. A paralytic squint is referred urgently for neurological assessment, and a non-paralytic squint to ophthalmology services. The College of Optometrists treats acute onset squint, new, sudden or worse, as an emergency within 24 hours.
faq.q: When should a child with a squint be referred?

faq.a: In Scotland's orthoptist-led screening of children aged 3.5 to 5.5, strabismus, intermittent included, was found in 2.00% in 2020–21 and 2.19% in 2021–22. The authors note this is close to the Royal College of Ophthalmologists' figure of 2.1% for children, and that their sample was mainly Caucasian. These are screening results from eight health boards, not diagnoses.
faq.q: How common is squint in children in the UK?

faq.a: Not in the UK. Orthoptists are trained to refract and some do, mostly young children by cycloplegic retinoscopy in hospital clinics, but the Opticians Act allows only optometrists and registered medical practitioners to issue a spectacle prescription, so an ophthalmologist or optometrist signs it. In a 2025 study for the General Optical Council, focus groups of 16 eye care professionals and students were open to changing that in hospitals, with training and consultant supervision.
faq.q: Can an orthoptist prescribe glasses?

body.text: In Scotland, orthoptists screen the vision of children aged 3.5 to 5.5, and the screening looks for more than blur. [A study in Ophthalmic and Physiological Optics](https://doi.org/10.1007/s44402-026-00042-2), published online in March, analysed five years of that screening from eight health boards. Squint, intermittent included, was found in 1.42% of children screened in 2013–14 and 2.19% in 2021–22, and binocular vision anomalies as the study defined them rose from 3.02% to 4.89%.

For a UK optometrist that turns orthoptist vs optometrist into a practical question. A child with a turn in the eye can reach either profession first, and the referral rules decide where the child goes next and how fast.
What the study did

Since 2013, See4School has invited every child in Scotland registered with a GP, and not already under the hospital eye service, to screening by an orthoptist. Evans and colleagues used the eight health boards that returned data every year, which cover over 85% of Scotland's population, for 2013–14 to 2015–16 and 2020–21 to 2021–22: between 35,643 and 42,431 children a year. Each child had a cover test at distance and near and an eye movement check. Its binocular vision anomalies include strabismus, esophoria, some exophoria and eye movement problems. These are screening results, not diagnoses.
What was found

It rose every year studied, 3.02%, 3.78%, 3.83%, 4.87% and 4.89%, but most of the rise fell across the four years with no data. Two things drove it. Squint rose from 1.42% to 2.19%, mostly intermittent exotropia, which more than doubled from 0.43% to 0.98%, while esotropia stayed near 1% (0.88% in 2013–14, 1.05% in 2021–22). And esophoria doubled, from 1.06% to 2.22%.
The authors suggest rising myopia, already reported from the same programme, as the reason exotropia is increasing.

In 2013–14, 342 children had a binocular vision anomaly and presenting vision good enough to pass a letter-chart screen, and 512 did in 2021–22: between 23.2% and 32.7% of the anomalies found each year.
Orthoptist vs optometrist: who does what

Orthoptists specialise in eye movements and binocular vision, work mainly in hospital eye departments alongside ophthalmologists, and deliver children's vision screening where eye care professionals do it, as across Scotland. Some refract as well. [A 2025 study for the General Optical Council](https://doi.org/10.22599/bioj.384), two focus groups of 16 eye care professionals and students, found some orthoptists already refracting young children in hospital clinics, mostly by cycloplegic retinoscopy. The Opticians Act lets only optometrists and registered medical practitioners issue a spectacle prescription, so an ophthalmologist or optometrist signs it.

Optometrists see children in community practice, where the cover test belongs in every child's sight test. The evidence on their referrals is thin but encouraging. In [a 2023 review of optometrists' referral accuracy](https://doi.org/10.1111/opo.13183), the one UK study of children's binocular vision referrals found that 88.9% of 45 optometrist referrals matched the hospital's diagnosis in full or in part, against 65% of GP referrals. [Earlier pieces on referral from community practice](/news) cover the adult side.
When a squint needs referring, and how fast

[NICE's guideline on suspected neurological conditions](https://www.nice.org.uk/guidance/ng127/chapter/recommendations-for-children-aged-under-16) sets four rules for children. A new squint with loss of the red reflex in either eye goes to ophthalmology immediately. A new squint with ataxia, vomiting or headache goes to acute paediatric services immediately. A paralytic squint is referred urgently for neurological assessment, even without other signs of raised intracranial pressure. A non-paralytic squint is referred to ophthalmology services.

[The College of Optometrists' urgency table](https://www.college-optometrists.org/clinical-guidance/guidance/guidance-annexes/annex-4-urgency-of-referrals-table) puts acute onset squint or nerve palsy, new, sudden or worse, in its emergency column, within 24 hours, so a new paralytic squint falls under both. NICE gives no timescale for a non-paralytic squint without those signs, and in my view a long-standing one found at a routine test can go as a routine referral, with the findings the orthoptist will need.
Why it matters in practice

items: Cover test every child at distance and near. In the Scottish data, up to a third of the binocular anomalies came with vision good enough to pass a letter chart.
Intermittent exotropia more than doubled in the Scottish data, and because it comes and goes, ask the parents when the eye drifts and whether they have a photograph of it.
Onset decides the speed: whether the squint is new, sudden or worse, whether it is paralytic, the red reflex, and headache, vomiting or unsteadiness.
Write the letter the orthoptist needs: direction, constant or intermittent, distance and near, onset, visual acuity, the refraction and whether it was cycloplegic, and the red reflex.

body.text: The caveats

items: These are screening records, not diagnoses, and the study had no data on false negatives.
Scotland only, eight of 15 health boards and a mainly Caucasian sample, with no data for 2016 to 2020. Fewer eligible children attended after the pandemic, and screening in 2020–21 ran late.
The study had funding support from Hoya, and two authors have received research and consultancy funding from Hoya Vision Care.
The referral accuracy figure is one UK study of 45 referrals, and the refraction findings come from two focus groups of 16 eye care professionals and students.

body.text: Patient satisfaction with opticians is high in the UK, and it rose this year. In the [General Optical Council's 2026 public perceptions survey](https://optical.org/resource/public-perceptions-research-2026.html) of 2,014 adults, 89% of the 1,676 people who had a sight test in the last two years were satisfied with their overall experience, up from 87% in 2025. The report also shows what people rated lowest and who was least satisfied.
It is [National Eye Health Week](https://www.visionmatters.org.uk/) (21 to 27 September), a good week to hear from the people who already come in.
What the survey did

This wave was carried out online by DJS Research between 9 February and 2 March 2026, with 2,014 people aged 16 and over. The results are weighted to the UK population by age, gender and nation. The satisfaction questions went to the 1,676 people who had a sight test in the last two years, 83% of them at a high street practice and 15% in a hospital.
Patient satisfaction with opticians: what scored lowest

The examination scores well. 92% were satisfied with the optometrist who carried out their sight test, 91% that they were treated with care and compassion, 89% with how long they waited for the appointment, and 84% with how involved they were in decisions about their care.

Value for money scored lowest, at 76%, and at 70% among 16 to 24 year olds. Of the people who bought glasses or contact lenses, 20% agreed they had felt pressure to buy particular brands or types, down from 24% in 2025, and 73% said the price they expected matched the price they paid. Buying eyewear is harder to read: 72% were satisfied, but that is out of everyone with a recent test, and only 74% of them bought anything. Just 4% said they were dissatisfied.
Who is least satisfied

The report says the youngest adults, people from ethnic minority backgrounds and people with at least one vulnerability marker (a disability, a household income under £25,000, or struggling financially, among others) were less likely than average to be satisfied on almost every measure.

Age makes the biggest difference. The report uses different age bands for different questions: 16 to 24 for value for money, 16 to 34 for the rest. 82% of 16 to 34 year olds were satisfied that the optometrist gave them enough time to deal with their needs properly, against 91% of 35 to 64 year olds and 96% of people aged 65 and over, and overall satisfaction was 83% in the youngest group and 95% in the oldest. Part of that may be where they were seen: 30% of 16 to 34 year olds had their last test in a hospital, not a practice. For patients from ethnic minority backgrounds the widest gap was on the wait for an appointment, 80% satisfied against 92% of white patients, with 84% against 91% on the time they were given.
The complaints that are not made

Only 52 people in the survey were dissatisfied with their overall experience. Of those, 15% said they complained, 35% considered it and decided not to, and 46% did not consider it. The researchers flag this as a very small base, so the proportions are rough. It suggests a complaints file may miss much of what the least satisfied patients think.
After the referral

The GOC survey does not ask about referral. A separate, self-selecting survey by [Healthwatch England](https://www.healthwatch.co.uk/report/2025-03-20/strain-sight-waiting-nhs-specialist-eye-care) does, of people waiting for, or recently treated in, NHS specialist eye care in England between July and September 2024. Of the 471 people still waiting, 70% had noticed their vision get worse during the wait, and 14% said they knew who to contact for further information. 85% said they would trust an optician to refer them directly without seeing a GP first. Denmark has tried [a pathway where consultants review practice scans remotely](/news/denmark-oct-teleophthalmology-referrals).
Why it matters in practice

items: Say what the sight test costs before the appointment. Those who knew beforehand rated value for money a little higher (78%, against 76% overall), which is an association, not proof, but it costs nothing.
Look at who waits longest for an appointment. The widest gap for patients from ethnic minority backgrounds was on the wait itself.
Watch the time given to younger patients, and check the explanation landed. They were among the less satisfied on both.
Ask. In a small sample, most patients who were dissatisfied did not complain, so a question at collection may pick up what the complaints file misses.
When you refer, tell the patient what happens next and who to contact. In the Healthwatch survey, 14% of those waiting knew who to contact.

body.text: The caveats

items: Both are surveys of what people report, not measures of clinical care.
The GOC survey was run online through a consumer panel, and its questionnaire was redesigned this year.
The complaints figures rest on 52 people.
The Healthwatch survey was self-selecting and covered England only, so it describes the people who chose to answer.
The subgroup differences are the ones the report calls statistically significant; it does not rank every group on every measure.

keyPoints: 79 Danish optician stores examined 1,220,082 people between March 2022 and May 2025, before, during and after OCT was installed, with a consultant reviewing uncertain findings remotely.
Referrals into public eye care rose from 0.55% to 1.74% of those examined. Acute referrals were stable; subacute rose 178% and routine 292%.
The authors credit the whole pathway, not the scanner: standardised OCT, consultant review and structured triage together.
The UK has the scanners. What many practices still lack is someone at the other end of an uncertain scan.

faq.a: An OCT scan images the retina and the optic nerve head in cross-section, so it shows fluid, membranes, holes and thinning that the standard examination cannot. In the Danish stores it picked up central serous chorioretinopathy, epiretinal membrane, macular hole and wet AMD that the standard examination had not been finding at that rate, and it documents the drusen and atrophy of [dry AMD](/news/the-silent-epidemic-addressing-the-unmet-need-in-dry-amd), for which community practice has had little to offer.
faq.q: What does an OCT scan at the opticians detect?

faq.a: In Denmark they came with more, and mostly of the kind that can be planned. Referrals rose from 0.55% to 1.74% of those examined; acute referrals were stable, and the increase was subacute and routine cases. The authors say the rise belongs to OCT inside a pathway of standardised scanning, consultant review and triage, and should not be read as the scanner's effect alone.
faq.q: Do OCT scans at the opticians mean more referrals?

faq.a: The remote review of eye images and findings by an ophthalmologist. In the Danish model an optometrist uploads the OCT scans they are unsure about to a service where a consultant reviews them and decides between no follow-up, a review in the store, follow-up by the service, or referral into the public eye-care system, usually a practice-based ophthalmologist.
faq.q: What is teleophthalmology?

faq.a: Most appear to. Optometry Scotland's 2025 survey found 80% of Scottish practices have one, all but one of the 74 General Ophthalmic Services practices in Bristol's catchment did, and the largest multiple has one in every store. What varies is what happens next: a hospital-reviewed pathway like Bristol's exists in some areas and not in others. The Danish result came from OCT inside a consultant-reviewed pathway, and the authors decline to separate the two.
faq.q: Do opticians in the UK offer OCT scans?

body.text: Between March 2022 and May 2025, 1,220,082 people had an eye examination in one of the 79 stores of a Danish optician chain, before, during and after each store installed an OCT scanner connected to a consultant-reviewed teleophthalmology service. [A study published on 15 September in the European Journal of Ophthalmology](https://doi.org/10.1177/11206721261488973), from an 18-author group led from the University of Copenhagen, reports what that did to referrals. They went up, by a lot, and the interesting part is where.

For a UK optometrist the question is no longer whether to own an OCT; [Optometry Scotland's survey last year](https://www.aop.org.uk/ot/news/2025/09/16/optometry-scotland-calls-for-oct-to-be-integrated-into-primary-eye-care-in-scotland) found 80% of Scottish practices already do. It is what happens to the public eye service when a whole high street starts scanning through a pathway that already has a consultant reading the doubtful cases. Denmark has now watched that happen at national scale, in one chain, with no comparison against OCT on its own.
What the study did

It is a nationwide, multi-period observational study of one optometry chain. Every examination in the 79 stores was counted across three periods: before OCT arrived, while it was being rolled out, and after it was in every store. Findings the optometrist was unsure about went to a teleophthalmology service, where a consultant ophthalmologist reviewed the images and the case was triaged: no follow-up, follow-up in the store, follow-up by the service, or referral into the public healthcare system, graded acute, subacute or routine. In Denmark that referral usually goes to a practice-based ophthalmologist, a tier the UK does not have, who gatekeeps the hospital.

The chain is not new to this. The same group described the pathway in 2021, before OCT: in one year, from a pool of 386,361 customers, 9,938 people were sent to the telemedical service, and 80.5% of them were kept out of the national eye care system; 14.4% needed no follow-up at all.
What the OCT scans did to referrals

Monthly submissions to the teleophthalmology service rose from 703 before OCT to 2,359 after full implementation, more than three times as many. Referrals into public healthcare rose from 0.55% to 1.74% of those examined.

The shape of that increase is the finding. Acute referrals were stable. Subacute referrals rose by 178% and routine referrals by 292%. Detection of central serous chorioretinopathy, epiretinal membrane, macular hole and neovascular AMD all increased markedly. The scanner did not flood the emergency clinic; it sent in more suspected disease of the kind that can wait a few weeks, with time to plan.

The authors are careful about attribution. The changes, they write, belong to an integrated model: OCT imaging, standardised acquisition by the optometrist, consultant review and structured triage, together. Not to the OCT on its own.
Why it matters in practice

The scale is what makes this useful. An earlier paper from the same group counted 355,818 different people imaged in the stores in a single year: 5.99% of Denmark's population, and between 8% and 9% of each decade from 41 to 80. Few programmes image six per cent of a population in a year. A high street with OCT and somewhere to send the scan did.

The UK has the scanners. What it mostly lacks is the layer. Where something like it exists, as in [a Bristol pathway published in August](https://doi.org/10.1007/s40123-026-01477-z), community optometrists sent OCT volume scans and fundus photographs for review by a consultant or a hospital optometrist within one working day; 87.0% of 376 macular referrals were appropriate, 73.7% of those avoided the first hospital visit the old pathway required, and wet AMD was treated in a mean of 8.6 days. In Scotland, Optometry Scotland asked last September for a General Ophthalmic Services fee for OCT in acute presentations and capital funding for the scanners. In England, June's £20 million to give every NHS-contracted practice access to the e-Referral service by April 2028 is part of the plumbing such a layer needs: it carries the referral, not the scan.

For a practice, the practical reading is this. When your OCT finds something you are not sure about, is there a consultant at the other end of a secure upload, or only a referral letter? Ask your local eye service which it is. A Danish modelling study put the cost per suspected posterior-segment case at £116 through a general ophthalmologist and £75 to £94 through the teleophthalmology route, with a wait of 25 weeks against under six. Those are Danish figures for a Danish system, and the model predates OCT and assumed the pathway would cut referrals, where the new study shows them rising. What it prices is the review layer, and that direction is not subtle.
The caveats

items: Observational, in one chain, and written by the team that runs the service. It is not a randomised comparison.

More detection is not the same as better outcomes. The study counts referrals and diagnoses, not sight saved, and more routine referrals for epiretinal membrane also means more people told about something that may never need treatment.
Denmark's chain, public eye service and fees are not the NHS, and the cost figures come from a model, not from the pathway's accounts.
The full paper is behind a paywall. The figures here are from its abstract and from the group's open-access earlier papers.
